questions.q: Why does the lesson say a model's builder shouldn't be the sole approver for production deployment once the stakes go up?
options: One person can't see their own blind spots, and nobody else is accountable if they're wrong — the same issue as self-approving a production database change
Builders are generally untrustworthy and need constant supervision
Only external auditors are legally allowed to approve models
Builders are not technically capable of evaluating their own models
questions.explain: The lesson frames this as a blind-spot and accountability problem, not a trust problem — the same reasoning used for other self-approval anti-patterns.

questions.q: What are the five typical approval gates the lesson describes, in order?
options: Development, technical validation, risk/compliance review, business sign-off, production approval
Marketing, sales, legal, finance, HR
Training, testing, deployment, monitoring, retirement only, with no sign-offs
A single gate: whether the model's accuracy is above 90%
questions.explain: The lesson lists these five gates explicitly, each checking something different before a version can be promoted.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what does a technical validation reviewer actually check?
options: The evaluation methodology itself — whether the test set was properly held out and the metric is appropriate
Whether the model's code is written in Python or R
The model's marketing copy
Whether the model was trained on a weekend or a weekday
questions.explain: Technical validation is specifically about methodology — a valid held-out test set and an appropriate metric — not style or scheduling details.

questions.q: Which of these is listed in the lesson as a common real reason an approval gets rejected?
options: The evaluation metric doesn't match what the business actually cares about
The model's file name is too long
The model was trained using a cloud provider instead of on-premises hardware
The approver personally dislikes the model's name
questions.explain: A metric/business-cost mismatch is one of the lesson's listed common rejection reasons, along with an incomplete model card, uneven subgroup performance, and a missing registry owner.

questions.q: How does the lesson say the depth of an approval workflow should scale?
options: The depth of review should match the stakes — a low-risk model moves through gates quickly, a high-stakes one gets full scrutiny at every gate
Every model, regardless of risk, must pass all five gates with identical, maximum scrutiny
Only models that fail their first evaluation need any review at all
Approval workflows should be skipped entirely for internal tools
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly says not every model needs all five gates at full weight — review depth should match the stakes of the decision.
